name: Lan Xang
summary: A Lao kingdom, the “land of a million elephants”, that held present-day Laos for three and a half centuries and is the basis of Laos’s national identity.

location.value: Present-day Laos and parts of north-east Thailand, along the Mekong.

terrain.value: The Mekong River carried its trade and shaped its political geography; mountains and forest elsewhere.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon, with a wet and a dry season.

resources.value: Forest products, gold, elephants and rice grown along the Mekong.

disasters.value: Unknown in detail; floods along the Mekong.

population.value: No reliable estimate; a 1376 census reportedly counted 300,000 Lao men.

urbanisation.value: Luang Prabang was the capital until 1560, then Vientiane.

migration.value: Tai-Lao peoples settled the Mekong valleys.

economicBase.value: Rice farming and river trade in forest products.

tradeRoutes.value: Mekong river trade linking China, Siam and Cambodia.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Bar-shaped silver and copper money; tribute from mueang.

inequality.value: King and nobles above villagers and slaves.

governmentType.value: Monarchy exercising authority through local lords (mueang) bound to the king, not a centralised territory.

keyRulers.value: Fa Ngum (founder, 1353), Setthathirath (moved the capital to Vientiane, 1560), Sourigna Vongsa (1638–1694, golden age).

succession.value: Hereditary, often disputed; disputes led to the 1707 split.

stability.value: Burmese invasions in the 16th century; long peace under Sourigna Vongsa.

eliteConflict.value: Succession disputes after Sourigna Vongsa’s death.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry and war elephants (“a million elephants”).

majorWars.value: Invaded several times by Burma in the 16th century; wars with Đại Việt (1479).

territoryChange.value: Partitioned in 1707 into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and (1713) Champasak.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals included Burma, Ayutthaya and Đại Việt; sometimes allied with Ayutthaya against Burma.

scienceEducation.value: Monasteries taught boys to read and copied palm-leaf manuscripts.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism was the state religion.

languageWriting.value: Lao, written in the Lao script; Pali for Buddhist texts.

artsArchitecture.value: Wat Xieng Thong (Luang Prabang) and Pha That Luang (Vientiane).

sharedIdentity.value: The basis of Laos’s national historic and cultural identity; the Phra Bang image was its palladium.

neighbours.value: Ayutthaya, Burma, Đại Việt and Cambodia.

ideasReligions.value: Theravada Buddhism, brought from Cambodia; the Emerald Buddha was kept in Vientiane.

colonisation.value: None; later states came under Siam and France.

riseSignals.value: Founded by Fa Ngum in 1353 with Khmer support.

peakPeriod.value: Under King Sourigna Vongsa (1638–1694), a time of peace and Buddhist learning.

declineSignals.value: A succession dispute after Sourigna Vongsa died in 1694 without a clear heir.

outcome.value: Split into the rival kingdoms of Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak (1707–1713).

sources.value: Lao chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Lan Xang”).
